idiom_name: Bunny exchanges + queue bindings (topic/direct/headers); in-process, a hash-of-lambdas or case dispatch over the header
implementation_notes: With Bunny the router is the exchange: messages are published to an exchange, never to a queue, and the broker routes them to every queue whose binding matches the message's routing key - topic exchanges match dotted keys with * (one word) and # (zero or more), direct exchanges require exact equality, fanout ignores the key and headers exchanges match on message attributes. That removes the router class entirely: the routing rules are queue.declare/bind calls and the publishers only need the routing key. Use the in-process form (a case statement over the message header, or a Hash of lambdas) only when the system has no broker, and keep the routing function separate from the consumers so it stays unit-testable.
code_sketch:
conn = Bunny.new; conn.start
ch   = conn.create_channel
x    = ch.topic('logs')                              # routing lives in the broker

q = ch.queue('', exclusive: true).bind(x, routing_key: 'kern.*')
q.subscribe do |_info, _props, payload|
  handle(payload)                                    # already selected for us
end

x.publish(line, routing_key: 'kern.critical')        # unmodified payload
pitfalls: A Bunny::Channel is not thread-safe: never publish a routing key from several threads on one channel - use one channel per thread or a channel pool.
Unroutable messages are dropped unless the mandatory flag or an alternate exchange is configured, so a broken binding looks like silence.
Bindings outlive the process: a non-exclusive queue keeps accumulating routed messages after its consumer exits.
A channel-level protocol error (for example publishing to a missing exchange) closes the whole channel, so the router needs recover_from_connection_close or explicit reconnection logic.
